\chapter{Wanting, Allowing, Wishing}
\label{ch:te-wanting-allowing-wishing}
\hlchaptermodality{80}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I want in Telugu, report what I think, give or refuse permission, invite somebody in, and offer congratulations.}

Complete TE-C80-congratulations and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nāku kāvāli]{\te{నాకు} \te{కావాలి} (nāku kāvāli) — I want it}

\label{lesson:TE-C80-want}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{gāru} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నాకు} \te{కావాలి}}
\textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{కావాలి}} (\emph{nāku kāvāli}) — \textquotedblleft{}I want it\textquotedblright{}. The new word in it is \textbf{\te{కావాలి}}, \textquotedblleft{}is wanted\textquotedblright{}.

You already have \textbf{\te{వద్దు}}, \textquotedblleft{}no, I don't want it\textquotedblright{}, which left you able to refuse a thing and unable to ask for one. \te{కావాలి} is the missing half.

\textbf{\te{నాకు} \te{టీ} \te{కావాలి}} — \textquotedblleft{}I want tea.\textquotedblright{} The wanter sits in the dative \te{నాకు}, exactly like the knower of \te{తెలుసు} and the liker of \te{ఇష్టం}. It is the same Telugu design a fourth time.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A request, and the opposite of \te{వద్దు}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kāvāli}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kāvāli}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nāku ṭī kāvāli}, then refuse it with \emph{vaddu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{nāku teliyadu}, then \emph{ivāḷa}, then \emph{telusu}, then say \emph{nāku kāvāli}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నాకు} \te{కావాలి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}I want it\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ani]{\te{అని} (ani) — that (reporting what was said or thought)}

\label{lesson:TE-C80-that}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāvāli} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అని}}
\textbf{\te{అని}} (\emph{ani}) — the little word that closes a quotation.

You already have \textbf{\te{అనుకో}}, \textquotedblleft{}to think\textquotedblright{}, with nothing it could think \emph{about}. \te{అని} is what attaches a thought or a sentence to the verb.

It comes \textbf{after} what is being reported, not before it: \textbf{\te{తెలుగు} \te{సులభం} \te{అని} \te{అనుకుంటాను}} — \textquotedblleft{}I think that Telugu is easy\textquotedblright{}, literally \textquotedblleft{}Telugu-is-easy \emph{that} I-think\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Telugu quotes forwards, not backwards}]
English opens with \emph{that} and then reports. Telugu reports and then closes with \te{అని}. The quoted sentence keeps its own shape completely — nothing inside it changes — and \te{అని} is the seam. Every reported thought, every reported question and every reported instruction in Telugu is built this way, so this one syllable opens the whole of indirect speech.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second clause, hanging off a verb of thinking or saying.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ani}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ani}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{telugu sulabhaṁ ani anukuṇṭānu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{arthaṁ kālēdu}, then \emph{ninna}, then \emph{uṇḍu}, then say \emph{ani}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అని} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}that (reporting what was said or thought)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[veḷḷavaccu]{\te{వెళ్ళవచ్చు} (veḷḷavaccu) — you may go}

\label{lesson:TE-C80-may}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ani} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{వెళ్ళవచ్చు}}
\textbf{\te{వచ్చు}} (\emph{vaccu}) — \textquotedblleft{}may\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}is allowed to\textquotedblright{}, and also \textquotedblleft{}can\textquotedblright{}.

It is the same \te{వచ్చు} you met as \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}, doing a second job: what \emph{comes} to you is what you may do.

\textbf{\te{వెళ్ళవచ్చు}} — \textquotedblleft{}you may go\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\te{వెళ్ళవచ్చా}?} — \textquotedblleft{}may I go?\textquotedblright{}, with the -\te{ఆ} of the last chapter. To refuse, the answer is \textbf{\te{వద్దు}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Permission: asking for it, giving it, refusing it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vaccu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vaccu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask \emph{veḷḷavaccā?}, then allow it, then refuse it
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{unnārā}, then \emph{eppuḍu vastāru?}, then \emph{tinu}, then say \emph{veḷḷavaccu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{వెళ్ళవచ్చు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}you may go\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lōpaliki raṇḍi]{\te{లోపలికి} \te{రండి} (lōpaliki raṇḍi) — please come in}

\label{lesson:TE-C80-comein}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vaccu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{లోపలికి} \te{రండి}}
\textbf{\te{రండి}} (\emph{raṇḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}please come\textquotedblright{}.

\te{రా} was the blunt \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} you say to a friend. Add the respectful \textbf{-\te{అండి}} and it becomes what you say at your own door to anybody.

With \te{స్వాగతం} it is the whole of a Telugu welcome: \textbf{\te{రండి}, \te{స్వాగతం}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An invitation, in the register you would actually use it in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{raṇḍi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{raṇḍi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{raṇḍi}, then \emph{svāgataṁ}, then \emph{kūrcōṇḍi}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{snēhituḍi}, then \emph{mundu}, then \emph{ivvu}, then say \emph{lōpaliki raṇḍi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{లోపలికి} \te{రండి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}please come in\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śubhākāṅkṣalu]{\te{శుభాకాంక్షలు} (śubhākāṅkṣalu) — congratulations, good wishes}

\label{lesson:TE-C80-congratulations}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{raṇḍi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{శుభాకాంక్షలు}}
\textbf{\te{శుభాకాంక్షలు}} (\emph{śubhākāṅkṣalu}) — \textquotedblleft{}good wishes\textquotedblright{}, which is Telugu for \textquotedblleft{}congratulations\textquotedblright{}.

You have been building it for six chapters without knowing. \textbf{\te{శుభ}} is the \emph{auspicious} of \te{శుభోదయం} and \te{శుభ} \te{రాత్రి}; \textbf{\te{ఆకాంక్ష}} is a wish; \textbf{-\te{లు}} is the plural ending you met in your very first lesson.

\textbf{\te{జన్మదిన} \te{శుభాకాంక్షలు}} is \textquotedblleft{}happy birthday\textquotedblright{}. Said alone it covers a wedding, an examination passed, a new house — anything worth marking.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The last thing this book teaches you to say, and the kindest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{śubhākāṅkṣalu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{śubhākāṅkṣalu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{śubhōdayaṁ}, then \emph{śubhākāṅkṣalu}, and hear the śubha in both
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mā}, then \emph{saṁvatsaraṁ}, then \emph{ikkaḍa}, then say \emph{śubhākāṅkṣalu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{శుభాకాంక్షలు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}congratulations, good wishes\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
